extracted.intended_audience: writers and students of fiction; critics and teachers of the craft of fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on choosing and managing narrative method and point of view in fiction — when to use scenic/dramatic presentation vs pictorial/omniscient narration, how to prepare characters for crises, and how first/third/oblique narration affect scope and voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose method dictated by subject
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select dramatic/scenic or pictorial/omniscient methods according to what the theme requires — do not force a writer’s preferred method on a story whose subject needs a different treatment. The passage repeatedly emphasizes that whether to dramatize or to picture is decided by the demands of the material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use strict scenic/dramatic form when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: In the novel of pure drama the point of view is that of the reader alone ... there is no 'going behind' the characters, no direct revelation of their thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For purely dramatic subjects present action episode-by-episode, avoid authorial intrusions and interior commentary, and let motives be transmuted into observable action; this yields compactness, objectivity, and theatrical 'rightness' but sacrifices access to private consciousness and panoramic survey.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow narrator to 'enter' characters' minds sparingly to aid a scene
rubrics_metrics.description: Tolstoy ... never hesitates to lay bare the mind of any of his people, at any moment, if it seems to help the force or the lucidity of the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even within a primarily scenic approach, occasional direct revelation of thought can clarify or intensify a scene; use such intrusions only when they enhance force or lucidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide adequate preparation before dramatic turning-points
rubrics_metrics.description: If she is so soon to be seen at this pitch of exaltation, it is essential that her life should be fully shared by the onlooker; but ... Anna is in the midst of her crisis and has passed it before it is possible to know her life clearly from within.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the reader has sufficient shared experience and intimacy with a character before placing them in a major emotional or pivotal action; otherwise the action will seem abrupt or arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: When an opening must summarize a situation, use condensation/concentration
rubrics_metrics.description: The space it may cover must be tightly packed; the method should be that which most condenses and concentrates the representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a narrative must convey a character's past and context quickly (for instance because the action must start immediately), favor summarizing/condensing methods (as Balzac might) rather than leisurely scenic episodes that fail to prepare the situation adequately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enrich character by inserting vivid small scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: A passing glimpse of this kind ... in half a page he makes an unforgettable scene. The half-page is not a diversion or an interlude; it speeds the story by augmenting the tone and the value of the lives that we are watching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concise, evocative micro-scenes to accumulate detail and deepen the reader’s impression of characters over time; such moments add tone and reality without derailing the main action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use an internal narrator to dramatize authorial assertion
rubrics_metrics.description: If the story-teller is in the story himself, the author is dramatized; his assertions gain in weight, for they are backed by the presence of the narrator in the pictured scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of making naked authorial statements, present a narrator/observer within the fiction to bear assertions and give them visible authority; this shifts responsibility into the story-world and reduces arbitrary-author intrusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer showing a narrator’s consciousness in the moment over retrospective report when introspection is central
rubrics_metrics.description: If he is himself the subject of his story ... far better it would be to see him while his mind is actually at work in the agitation, whatever it may be, which is to make the book. The matter would then be objective and visible to the reader, instead of reaching him in the form of a report at second hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the main interest is exploration of a consciousness (a soul-study), render the character’s mind in action at the moment rather than relying mainly on after-the-fact narration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the trade-offs of rigid dramatization
rubrics_metrics.description: The dramatic story ... is limited to so much as the ear can hear and the eye see. In rigid drama ... there is naturally no admission of the reader into the private mind of any of the characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that pure scenic dramatization grants objectivity and compactness but sacrifices interior access and panoramic scope; choose accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictorial (panoramic) method requires a narrator but can use dramatic enactment
rubrics_metrics.description: In a pictorial book the principle of the structure involves a point of view which is not the reader’s. It is open to the pictorial book, however, to use a method in its picture-making that is really no other than the method of drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when the work is essentially pictorial/retrospective (an impression or panorama), you can often achieve vividness by distributing the subject among characters and letting moments 'act' rather than only summarizing — blending picture and drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: First person fixes point of view in space/time; third person grants temporal freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: Now if he speaks in the first person there can, of course, be no uncertainty in the point of view; he has his fixed position ... But it need not be forfeited, it is clear, if the first person is changed to the third. The author may use the man’s field of vision and keep as faithfully within it as though the man were speaking for himself. In that case ... it is free in time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use first person when you want an unmistakably limited, single perspective with a fixed experiential 'edge'; use third person (anchored to a character) to keep that focused vision while gaining temporal mobility (retrospect, present urgency, gradations in time).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use oblique (free indirect) narration to blend authorial and character perspectives
rubrics_metrics.description: The seeing eye is with somebody in the book, but its vision is reinforced; the picture contains more, becomes richer and fuller, because it is the author’s as well as his creature’s ... there are now two brains behind that eye ... there are touches in it that go beyond any sensation of his, and indicate that some one else is looking over his shoulder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply oblique/free indirect style to retain the apparent vantage of a character while subtly supplementing it with the author’s perception — this deepens the picture without obvious shifts in point of view and reduces the insistent sound of the narrator’s voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inconsistent mixing of points of view
rubrics_metrics.description: To glance upon the story from a height and to give a general impression of its course — this is at once to remove the point of view from the reader and to set up a new one somewhere else; the method is no longer consistent, no longer purely dramatic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain consistency in how and when point-of-view shifts occur; indiscriminate or ill-timed shifts (e.g., moving between reader-only scenic view and distant authorial panorama) produce methodological inconsistencies and weaken effect.
